evidence.heading: Why expert parallelism needs a communication layer
evidence.sectionLabel: Why expert parallelism needs a communication layer
evidence.quote: Start from one rank's view. A rank is a process in the communication group; here each rank controls one GPU. An MoE architecture replaces one dense feed-forward block with many expert blocks. A router chooses top-k experts for each token. evidence.heading: A four-token routing ledger
evidence.quote:
## A four-token routing ledger

Use two ranks and four tokens. Rank 0 owns tokens `a` and `b`; rank 1 owns `c` and `d`. There are four experts, two per rank, and each token selects two experts. Here the two selected experts always live on different ranks, so eight expert slots also require eight source-token/destination-rank rows, including local rows.

| Token | Source rank | First expert | Second expert | Gate weights |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `a` | 0 | 0 (rank 0) | 3 (rank 1) | 0.70, 0.30 |
| `b` | 0 | 2 (rank 1) | 1 (rank 0) | 0.40, 0.60 |
| `c` | 1 | 1 (rank 0) | 3 (rank 1) | 0.55, 0.45 |
| `d` | 1 | 0 (rank 0) | 2 (rank 1) | 0.25, 0.75 |

Rank 0 sends one copy of `a` to expert 3 and one copy of `b` to expert 2. It also receives `c` for expert 1 and `d` for expert 0. Rank 1 performs the mirror exchange. The counts happen to balance here; a real gate can send more rows from one rank than that rank receives.

Read each copy in two coordinate systems:

1. **Source coordinates:** `(source_rank, token_index, topk_slot)` identify the original row and expert choice.
2. **Expert coordinates:** `(destination_rank, local_expert, expert_slot)` identify where a receiving GEMM expects the row.

evidence.heading: What callers actually use it for
evidence.quote: ### What callers actually use it for Follow one routed token through the graph and four kernel families answer different bottlenecks: 1. **Dense projection layers.** Attention and feed-forward layers reduce to matrix products. DeepGEMM exposes BF16 and low-bit GEMMs for these hot loops. 2. **Mixture-of-Experts.** Grouped GEMMs process the variable number of tokens sent to each expert. Contiguous and masked layouts target prefill and decode differences. 3. **DeepSeek indexer scoring.** MQA scoring turns query vectors, compressed key/value vectors, and per-head weights into token-to-token logits. The kernel has non-paged and paged forms for prefill and decode, with an FP4 indexer path in later releases.[^deepseek2025v32][^deepgemm2026mega] 4. **Expert-parallel inference.** Mega MoE combines dispatch, two expert projections, SwiGLU, and combine so NVLink traffic can overlap tensor-core work.[^deepgemm2026mega] The README also lists HyperConnection (HC) GEMMs. We won't trace every primitive: dense GEMM establishes the memory path, grouped GEMM adds uneven routing, and Mega MoE adds communication. The indexer is a useful contrast because its output isn't an expert activation or a full attention result.

### Worked routing example

Return to four of a Flash-shaped rank's 32 local experts. They receive `[64, 192, 32, 128]` routed rows. With M alignment 128, the contiguous pack reserves `[128, 256, 128, 128]` rows. evidence.heading: Grouped GEMM: the MoE shape problem
evidence.quote:
## Grouped GEMM: the MoE shape problem

An MoE layer routes each token to a small set of experts. Each expert sees a different number of tokens, so the straightforward choices are one GEMM per expert or padding every expert to the same M. Uneven routing makes each choice pay a different tax.

DeepGEMM's contiguous grouped API concatenates expert token segments into one M axis. N and K stay fixed because experts share weight dimensions. A compact layout tensor describes each segment, allowing one kernel to schedule multiple expert blocks while reusing one compiled implementation.

The segment boundaries still need alignment. The README requires each expert segment to meet the M block alignment returned by `get_mk_alignment_for_contiguous_layout()`. Padding belongs in the caller's token packing, and the resulting output must be unpacked to the original token order.

Read the configured alignment alongside `get_theoretical_mk_alignment_for_contiguous_layout()`. At the current snapshot, the configured default is 128, while the theoretical SM100 helper returns 256 and ignores `expected_m`.[^deepgemm2026OctoberSnapshot] For our four groups, alignment 256 would reserve 1,024 rows instead of 640. A theoretically favorable tile can therefore increase padding for small groups; the configured default remains 128.

| Grouped mode | Known at launch? | Layout | Intended workload |
|---|---|---|---|
| Contiguous | Expert token counts known | Concatenated M segments | Training and prefill |

evidence.heading: Mega MoE: overlap communication and compute
evidence.quote: ## Mega MoE: overlap communication and compute The data that can move is the next expert chunk's dispatch, while this chunk's tensor cores are busy. Mega MoE fuses expert-parallel dispatch, linear 1, SwiGLU, linear 2, and expert-parallel combine into one SM100 kernel. It uses PyTorch symmetric memory so ranks can address each other's buffers and overlap NVLink traffic with tensor-core work.[^deepgemm2026mega] The computation still follows ordinary MoE semantics: 1. Router selects top-k experts and weights for each token. 2. Expert parallelism dispatches token rows to owning ranks. 3. Linear 1 produces gate and up activations. 4. SwiGLU applies the gated activation. 5. Linear 2 projects back to the hidden size. 6. Combine returns weighted expert outputs to the source rank. Schedule and storage provide the core mechanism. A symmetric ring buffer holds token data, scale data, routing indices, weights, and intermediate expert activations. Persistent schedulers claim blocks, move remote data into reusable slots, run L1 and L2 work, and release slots only after all consumers finish.

evidence.excerpt: Suppose one query's KV history is split across two CTAs. What can each worker discard while still letting a parent recover exact attention? Normalization has to survive. An attention kernel normally looks like a matrix multiplication followed by a softmax and a value multiplication, but FlashAttention already showed that the full score matrix is unnecessary. evidence.heading: Core mechanism: schedule work around state
evidence.excerpt: If two workers process disjoint key ranges for the same query row and head, each returns an output vector $o$ and a base-2 log-sum-exp $b$. support.heading: Attention head masks
support.openingExcerpt:
Start with one attention layer. During estimation, every head still exists, but a scalar can turn its contribution up or down. If that scalar ends near zero, predict what happens next: the output is gated first; the head disappears only when the pruning helper slices its feature range.

Let layer `i` have `N_H` heads. A head output is multiplied by scalar `m_A^(i)`. For one head:

$$
h^{(i)}_j = m_{A,j}^{(i)} \cdot \operatorname{head}^{(i)}_j(X).
$$

When `m_A` is near zero, the head contributes little to the task loss under this early trajectory. The mask starts at one, so initial behavior matches the unmasked model. Gradient descent can move individual values, while an L1 term makes small values attractive. This signal applies to the current task and training trajectory; later training or tasks can change the head's value.

The repository implements this in `models/hf_roberta/modeling_roberta.py`. When `config.mask_training` is true, each attention block creates `early_attn_mask` shaped like `(1, heads, 1, 1)` and multiplies attention probabilities by it. evidence.quote: | Pressure | Axis or mechanism | What gets partitioned | Typical NCCL op | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Wide matrix doesn't fit | Tensor parallelism (TP) | A layer's weight and activation channels | All-reduce or all-gather | | Stack is too deep | Pipeline parallelism (PP) | Contiguous layer ranges | Point-to-point activation send/receive | | Batch needs throughput | Data parallelism (DP) | Independent samples or replicas | Gradient reduce or reduce-scatter | | Prompt is too long | Context parallelism (CP) | Sequence chunks and attention context | Peer-to-peer or collective KV exchange | | MoE experts are spread out | Expert parallelism (EP) | Expert weights and routed tokens | All-to-all dispatch and combine | | Activations fill memory | Selective recomputation | Saved intermediates | Extra forward compute, less storage | Read the table as a diagnosis map, not a menu of interchangeable flags. Each axis owns a different piece of state, so the same extra GPU can remove one bottleneck and add another. Follow one sample through a candidate mesh before choosing. Data parallelism keeps its computation on one replica. Tensor parallelism makes its layer arithmetic cross tensor shards. Pipeline parallelism sends its activation from one layer range to the next. Context parallelism keeps only part of its sequence local. Expert parallelism may move its routed token to another rank and back. That trace predicts where the next wait can appear.[^megatronCoreParallelism2026] The first budget is memory and the second is communication. TP lowers per-layer memory but adds collectives. DP raises independent work in flight without making one sample's path shorter. PP can make a model fit across nodes, but it inserts stage-to-stage latency. CP reduces sequence-local activation pressure while exchanging remote context. EP spreads expert weights while paying for token movement. Choose the smallest set of axes that removes the observed wall, then measure the new wait.

### Expert parallelism: split sparse capacity

An MoE layer has a router that chooses top-`k` experts for each token. Predict from a skewed route histogram: if most tokens choose one expert, the total token count hasn't changed, but one rank now owns a queue while others wait. Expert parallelism (EP) places different experts on different GPUs. The dispatcher permutes tokens, sends each token to its expert owners, runs grouped expert GEMMs, then sends outputs back and unpermutes them. Current dispatcher code exposes all-gather and all-to-all paths, plus Flex backends that can specialize communication, including a DeepEP path on supported NVIDIA GPUs.[^megatron2026moe]

With `k=2`, a token produces two routed assignments, not one. Suppose its selected experts return `[2,0]` and `[0,4]`, with router weights `0.75` and `0.25`. Combining gives `0.75 × [2,0] + 0.25 × [0,4] = [1.5,1]`. Returning both vectors to the original token position without applying the weights would change the model. The router's scoring and normalization policy determines those weights; they aren't necessarily uniform. A capacity-limited dispatcher may drop overflowing assignments, while dropless dispatch retains them and pays for the imbalance.[^megatron2026moe]

That prediction names EP's failure surface. An all-to-all can move every token to a different rank, while router skew produces hot experts, uneven work, padding, and queueing. Load-balancing loss, capacity policy, dropless dispatch, grouped GEMM, and overlapping communication with expert compute address different parts of that problem. They don't remove the need to inspect per-expert token counts and all-to-all timing.[^megatron2026moe]

evidence.quote: ## Distributed optimizer: trade replicated state for collectives The mesh decides where computation runs, but it doesn't decide who keeps every training byte. For conventional Adam with BF16 model parameters and FP32 main gradients, the guide's ledger is 18 bytes per parameter before activations and temporary buffers. The distributed optimizer changes it to $6 + 12/d$ bytes, where $d$ is the **optimizer sharding group's size**.[^megatron2026distopt] The six replicated bytes are two for a BF16 parameter and four for its main gradient buffer. The twelve shardable bytes are an FP32 master parameter and two FP32 Adam moments. These are bytes per parameter already assigned to this TP/PP shard, not necessarily per parameter of the entire model. At $d=4$, that gives nine bytes. In the running dense mesh, however, `DP=4` and `CP=2`; without hierarchical partitioning, the pinned implementation's DP-with-CP domain has eight ranks, so this ledger gives 7.5 bytes, not nine. Expert parameters can use a different domain. Inspect the actual optimizer group before substituting a number for $d$.[^megatron2026parallelstate] Trace one parameter's ownership across a step: 1. Backward fills a gradient buffer on each DP rank. 2. `reduce-scatter` combines gradients and gives each rank its shard, with scaling matched to the loss normalization. 3. Each rank updates its local FP32 master parameters and optimizer moments. 4. `all-gather` rebuilds the BF16 parameter buffer for the next forward. The parameter and gradient buffers are contiguous so communication can start as buckets become ready. Megatron can overlap gradient reduce-scatter with backward and parameter all-gather with forward when the configuration and backend support it. Overlap hides latency only when compute lasts long enough and the network isn't already saturated. evidence.quote: ### Context and sequence parallelism: split token work Sequence parallelism (SP) is a companion to TP, not another way to split a full attention calculation. evidence.quote: ## Distributed optimizer: trade replicated state for collectives The mesh decides where computation runs, but it doesn't decide who keeps every training byte. For conventional Adam with BF16 model parameters and FP32 main gradients, the guide's ledger is 18 bytes per parameter before activations and temporary buffers. The twelve shardable bytes are an FP32 master parameter and two FP32 Adam moments. Each rank updates its local FP32 master parameters and optimizer moments. 4. `all-gather` rebuilds the BF16 parameter buffer for the next forward. The parameter and gradient buffers are contiguous so communication can start as buckets become ready. support.heading: One step, one token budget
support.openingExcerpt: SRT maintains active requests and schedules a batch repeatedly. Decodes usually need one new token per request; prefills need many prompt tokens. Chunked prefill divides a long prompt so it doesn't monopolize a step while decodes wait. Exact flags and defaults change by release, so inspect `Scheduler.init_chunked_prefill` and the server arguments for the pinned commit. Use a simplified mixed-batch policy for the two classify requests. Shared prefix length is 4. `R0` is decoding (1 token); `R1` has 9 unmatched prompt tokens. With budget 6 and one decode token reserved, five `R1` prompt tokens fit: | Step | Ready work | Tokens admitted | State after step | | --- | --- | ---: | --- | | 0 | `R0` decode needs 1; `R1` prefill needs 9 | `R0=1`, `R1=5` | `R0` advances; `R1` has 4 prompt tokens left | | 1 | `R0` decode needs 1; `R1` prefill needs 4 | `R0=1`, `R1=4` | `R1` finishes prefill | | 2 | `R0` and `R1` decode | `R0=1`, `R1=1` | Both requests continue generation | Use this accounting example to understand mixed-chunk budgeting. At the pinned commit, `enable_mixed_chunk` defaults to false; when enabled, `PrefillAdder` subtracts mixed decode tokens from its input and chunk budgets. Admission also checks KV capacity, page alignment, and reservations for future output. Running both modes in one batch also depends on those admission checks.[^sglangPinnedSource2026]

support.heading: Insert, lock, evict
support.openingExcerpt:
A prefix cache needs ownership rules alongside its lookup map. While a request is active, its matched KV locations are protected. When a request finishes or releases a branch, nodes can become evictable. The eviction policy can be LRU or another configured strategy, but it must never reclaim state still referenced by a live request.

The source path is visible in `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/radix_cache.py`:

1. `match_prefix` finds the longest compatible path and returns KV indices.
2. `insert` adds a new token path after forward computation.
3. Lock and unlock operations protect prefixes while requests use them.
4. `evict` removes unprotected branches according to the selected policy.

This sequence exposes a common failure. If a request's KV reference is released too early, another request can overwrite memory while the first is still decoding. If references never drop, free KV capacity shrinks until admission stalls. Instrument active references, evictable tokens, match lengths, and allocator failures together.

support.heading: Parallelism and prefill-decode disaggregation
support.openingExcerpt: SGLang maps model work onto hardware through several parallelism axes. Before choosing one, predict the bottleneck: fitting weights, doing per-request compute, moving tokens between experts, or keeping decode local. Names vary by model, but the trade-offs are stable: | Axis | What is split | Helps with | Costs | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Tensor parallelism (TP) | Matrix dimensions across devices | Fit and per-request compute | Per-layer collectives | | Pipeline parallelism (PP) | Layer ranges across stages | Fit depth across nodes | Pipeline bubbles and stage sync | | Data parallelism (DP) | Full model replicas or request groups | Independent throughput | Weight memory and routing | | Expert parallelism (EP) | Mixture-of-Experts experts | Expert capacity and load balance | Token routing and all-to-all | | Context or sequence paths | Sequence positions or attention work | Long contexts and bandwidth | Extra communication and layout constraints | These choices have to align with attention backends, quantization, CUDA graphs, and model-specific layers. A TP setting that fits weights can still increase ITL if collective overhead dominates. A DP replica can raise throughput while lowering prefix-cache locality. SGLang's DP-attention path also differs from independent full-model replicas: attention can be data-parallel while other model parts remain sharded. Read the parallelism docs and benchmark the target topology before copying flags.[^sglang2026parallelism]
support.reason: Matrix dimensions, layers and request work are assigned across compute devices; the GPU is a numerical compute/memory resource, without claiming a hardware run.

support.heading: Runtime path: from API to model runner
support.openingExcerpt: A frontend expression and a plain HTTP payload look different at the edge. Inside SRT they share owners. Entrypoints parse requests; the tokenizer manager prepares model inputs and tracks request/output state. A separate detokenizer manager converts generated IDs to text in the usual multiprocess serving path. The scheduler plus radix cache decide which tokens run next and which KV locations already exist. The model runner loads weights, builds a forward batch, selects attention backends, and returns logits or sampled tokens.[^sglang2026docs] A delay before the first model batch suggests input, cache, or admission work. A delay between generated tokens can include scheduling, the runner, communication, grammar, speculation, and output delivery. TTFT includes the first forward pass and sampling too; these metrics don't divide neatly into CPU and GPU stages. The process split can vary with server mode and parallelism, but those responsibilities stay recognizable. Grammar and sampling code constrain or select the next token before the stream is updated. Follow the data, not a fixed process layout.

evidence.heading: Gate 3: bound async work
evidence.quote:
### Gate 3: bound async work

Set mini-batch size, generation-worker count, and `max_staleness_steps` together. Calculate completed-group plus in-flight headroom as $B(S+1)$, choose the pause mode (`keep`, `abort`, or `wait`), and check whether `use_cache_salt` isolates prefix-cache blocks across policy versions. Decide which trajectories are filtered as lag rises, how generation failures surface, and which metric stops the run automatically.

### Gate 4: keep a recovery packet

A replayable trajectory joins prompt, actions, observations, rewards, and policy version. Logs separate environment latency from inference latency. Require checkpoint saves to be atomic and resumable, and keep a rollback path for reward or sync regressions. Finally, name the offline slice that must pass before online gains count as learning.

> **🎯 Production tip:** Log trajectory ID, scheduled policy step, consumed policy step, reward components, stop reason, and environment revision together. A throughput chart without those joins fails to explain a bad update.

evidence.quote: ## Inference and weight synchronization The opening incident ends at the sampler. Check the recipe's server/router dependencies and actual generation **and control** endpoints before combining versions. An OpenAI-compatible chat response doesn't demonstrate pause/resume or weight-transfer support.[^skyrlPinnedDependencies2026][^vllm2026release0300]

evidence.heading: A worked policy update
evidence.quote: ## A worked policy update For a separate binary-reward SQL experiment, sample two queries for the same prompt. A frozen result checker gives the correct query reward 1 and the incorrect query reward 0. Their mean is $0.5$, giving centered advantages $+0.5$ and $-0.5$. This binary reward deliberately differs from the earlier shaped turn rewards. Choose the reward contract for the experiment and document how it maps into advantages and loss masks. With $y_+$ denoting the correct query and $y_-$ the incorrect one, the simplified loss encourages that change: $$ L = -\frac{1}{2}\left[(+0.5)\log \pi_\theta(y_+\mid x) + (-0.5)\log \pi_\theta(y_-\mid x)\right]. $$ That equation hides three implementation details: 1. The group must contain comparable samples for the same prompt. 2. The reward must be aligned with the environment's true success condition. 3. The loss mask must identify the response tokens that policy optimization should change. If both responses receive reward 1, the relative advantages are zero. That can mean an easy prompt or a broken evaluator. Inspect which case applies before changing the learning rate; more samples don't repair a checker that always returns success.

evidence.heading: Generator, environment, trainer
evidence.quote: Return to `query-42_0`. Before naming classes, predict what the trainer needs after two SQL turns: the sampled response, the database observation, the reward, and a way to distinguish trainable tokens from context. If that record is complete, the optimizer can stay unaware of whether the environment is SQL, a terminal, or a browser. A controller role sets up execution. A Generator coordinates inference and environments to produce trajectories. A Trainer turns those trajectories into gradients. Current control flow remains in `trainer.py`, while InferenceEngine and Environment stay replaceable boundaries inside the Generator. The loop isn't "model in, loss out." A multi-turn trajectory can include token IDs, tool calls, observations, rewards, per-token masks, and a stop reason. Those fields carry the decision from environment execution into optimization. Without them, a trainer can apply loss to an observation, credit a failed tool call as success, or join a retry to the wrong episode. ### Vocabulary at the seams The table is a decoder ring for the code. Read `Rollout` as the artifact being handed forward, and read the final column as the bug that appears when one boundary silently changes its meaning. | Term | Meaning here | Failure if misunderstood | |---|---|---| | Rollout | One model interaction or multi-turn trajectory collected from an environment | Treating a partial turn as a complete training example | | Generator | Component that turns prompts and environment configuration into trajectories | Putting task-specific loops inside the trainer | | Environment | State machine that consumes actions and emits observations, reward, and termination | Accepting unverified model-written scores | | Inference engine | Runtime that samples tokens and often returns log probabilities | Assuming the training model and sampler always share weights | | Training input | Tokenized prompt, response, masks, rewards, advantages, and metadata used by optimization | Applying loss to tool or padding tokens by accident | | Staleness | Difference between rollout scheduling step and consumption step | Optimizing on data generated by a policy far in the past | | Weight sync | Transfer of updated policy parameters to inference workers | Sampling with an old policy while labeling it on-policy | `GeneratorInput` includes prompts, environment classes, optional environment extras, sampling parameters, trajectory IDs, and batch metadata. `GeneratorOutput` returns batched prompt and response token IDs, rewards, loss masks, stop reasons, rollout metrics, optional log probabilities, trajectory IDs, and timing splits. It also includes step-wise completion flags and vision tensors. `TypedDict` describes the interface for type checkers; it doesn't validate a custom generator's arrays at runtime.[^skyrlPinnedGenerator2026] Here `Optional[...]` means a field's **value** may be `None`; it doesn't make that key optional. The pinned `TypedDict` uses required keys. A real extension must populate its declared fields, using `None` where appropriate, as well as preserve array alignment.[^skyrlPinnedGenerator2026]

evidence.heading: A token ledger between two engines
evidence.quote: ## A token ledger between two engines Start with a prediction. If one response contains model tokens, a tool observation, and more model tokens, what tells the trainer which positions deserve credit? A rollout acts as a ledger entry. Its prompt and sampled response carry the sequence, while log probabilities, loss masks, reward, status, and rollout ID explain how that sequence should affect the next gradient update. Ray decides where the ledger work runs. The Data Buffer keeps entries available until the trainer consumes a complete group. The policy appears twice, with different jobs. SGLang reads current weights and produces tokens quickly. Megatron reads those tokens and computes losses, gradients, and optimizer updates. A weight-sync operation is the commit that changes what SGLang will sample next. Delay that commit and data becomes off-policy by design, so timing must be recorded rather than inferred later. ```mermaid flowchart TB router["SGLang + custom rollout\nrouter / tools / env"]:::accent router --> buffer["Data Buffer\nSamples + groups"]:::warning buffer --> train["Megatron actor\nloss + optimizer"]:::primary train --> sync["Weight sync\npublish new policy"]:::success sync --> router ```

evidence.heading: SGLang and sgl-router own rollout
evidence.quote: ## SGLang and sgl-router own rollout At the rollout boundary, ask which representation can be trusted after a tool loop: decoded text or the IDs sampled by the policy? slime launches SGLang in server mode and keeps a router endpoint in front of its workers. A regular sample is tokenized, sent to `/generate` with `return_logprob=True`, and returned with response token IDs, per-token log probabilities, and metadata. Text helps an operator inspect a run; token IDs remain the training source of truth. The previous chapter's radix prefix cache still matters here. With `router_policy=consistent_hashing`, slime sends `X-SMG-Routing-Key` from the sample session ID, so one multi-turn session can return to the same worker and reuse its prefix cache. That improves locality, not provenance. The trajectory manager still has to prove which tokens came from the model. The default rollout function creates sample groups, runs generation concurrently, computes rewards, and waits until the requested batch is valid. Dynamic sampling can discard groups whose reward variation is unhelpful. Partial rollout mode can abort requests and keep unfinished samples for a later pass. SGLang's `/abort_request` endpoint supports that early stop when oversampling has already found enough valid responses.[^slime2025blog]

concepts.title: Evaluation row
concepts.meaning: One replayable graded case joining fixed inputs, observed behavior, grader evidence, and version pins.
concepts.brief: Receipt tile for fixture, output, grader, latency, and model pins; show one row separate from aggregate.
pitfalls: An aggregate is not a dataset snapshot.

concepts.title: Benchmark protocol
concepts.meaning: Versioned rules for task population, scoring, budget, and valid comparison.
concepts.brief: Boundary around benchmark tasks, harness, model snapshot, budget, and score.
pitfalls: Claims apply only to declared tasks and harness.

sourceRefs.title: Understanding SWE-bench
headings: Choose the benchmark before reading a score

concepts.title: Dataset split
concepts.meaning: Policy assigning examples to train, validation, and untouched test roles.
concepts.brief: Branch stable example IDs into split roles; tuning never touches final test.
pitfalls: Group/time/source leakage invalidates random splits.

sourceRefs.title: GLM-5.3 Training Masterclass
headings: Deduplicate before splitting, then test contamination again

concepts.title: Data lineage
concepts.meaning: Directed record linking sources, transformations, versions, owners, and artifacts.
concepts.brief: Graph source to transform to dataset to run/checkpoint to evaluation.
pitfalls: Lineage does not prove correctness or license.

concepts.title: Confidence interval
concepts.meaning: Range computed by a stated procedure to quantify sampling uncertainty.
concepts.brief: Show estimate, interval, and repeated-sampling intuition with assumptions.
pitfalls: Not a probability that this particular interval contains the parameter.

concepts.title: Probability calibration
concepts.meaning: Agreement between stated probabilities and observed frequencies.
concepts.brief: Reliability plot with bins, diagonal, sample counts, and miscalibration.
pitfalls: Calibration differs from ranking and depends on population.

concepts.title: Risk-coverage curve
concepts.meaning: Error among accepted cases as the system accepts a larger or smaller share.
concepts.brief: Move a reject threshold and animate accepted coverage with selective error.
pitfalls: Rejected cases need a safe path.

sourceRefs.title: Context Engineering: Beyond Prompting
headings: A summary must preserve the uncertainty

concepts.title: Ranking metrics
concepts.meaning: Distinct summaries of retrieval relevance, rank position, and recall.
concepts.brief: Animate recall@k, reciprocal rank, and average precision on one list.
pitfalls: No one metric substitutes for answer quality.

sourceRefs.title: Context Engineering: Beyond Prompting
headings: Retrieve the next fact you need

concepts.title: Judge agreement
concepts.meaning: Agreement between automated evaluators and human labels under one rubric.
concepts.brief: Two rubric cards grade identical cases; reveal discordant examples.
pitfalls: Agreement is consistency, not truth.

concepts.title: Causal effect
concepts.meaning: Outcome contrast under two interventions for a defined population and estimand.
concepts.brief: Treatment/control assignment, outcomes, contrast, assumptions.
pitfalls: Correlation alone is not causal identification.

concepts.title: Sequential test
concepts.meaning: Experiment analysis accounting for repeated looks at accumulating data.
concepts.brief: Evidence trajectory meets a predeclared stopping boundary.
pitfalls: Repeated ordinary fixed-sample p-values inflate false positives.

concepts.title: Statistical power
concepts.meaning: Probability a test detects a specified effect under a stated alternative and design.
concepts.brief: Overlay null/alternative curves, alpha/beta, sample-size effect.
pitfalls: Power is conditional on the assumed effect and design.

concepts.title: Release gate
concepts.meaning: Predeclared decision rule required before an artifact or system advances.
concepts.brief: Quality, safety, latency, and rollback checks converge with owners.
pitfalls: A gate does not replace monitoring.

concepts.title: Audit receipt
concepts.meaning: Evidence of actor, identity, policy, evidence, versions, and outcome.
concepts.brief: Receipt links actor, time, policy/model versions, evidence hashes, outcome.
pitfalls: Minimize private raw payloads.

sourceRefs.title: AI Lab System Design Interview
headings: Prompt 1: model gateway for enterprise teams
Preserve an audit trail without collecting everything

concepts.title: Request trace
concepts.meaning: Time-ordered linked spans through one request path.
concepts.brief: Request fans through retrieval/model/tool spans with parent links and failure location.
pitfalls: A trace describes one path, metrics aggregate populations.

concepts.title: Permission filter
concepts.meaning: Policy check limiting retrieved candidates to caller-authorized scope.
concepts.brief: Identity/query enters ACL filter; denied docs stop before packing.
pitfalls: Filtering after generation is too late.

sourceRefs.title: Context Engineering: Beyond Prompting
headings: Retrieval is also a permission boundary

concepts.title: Trust boundary
concepts.meaning: Crossing between components with different authority, identity, or data trust.
concepts.brief: Zone user/retriever/model/tool; mark enforced crossings and untrusted results.
pitfalls: Every crossing requires concrete enforcement.

concepts.title: Sandbox
concepts.meaning: Constrained execution limiting resources, filesystem/network access, and authority.
concepts.brief: Untrusted process inside explicit CPU/time/filesystem/network controls.
pitfalls: Containerization alone does not guarantee isolation.

sourceRefs.title: How to Build an AI Agent from Scratch
headings: Give the model a small, explicit world

concepts.title: Secret redaction
concepts.meaning: Detection and replacement/removal of credentials before exposure or storage.
concepts.brief: Scanner replaces matched credential with typed redaction marker.
pitfalls: Pattern scans miss secrets and can redact benign text.

concepts.title: Structured tool call
concepts.meaning: Typed request with schema-validated arguments and separately checked result.
concepts.brief: Proposal passes validation, authorization, execution, result normalization.
pitfalls: Valid JSON is not authorization.

sourceRefs.title: How to Build an AI Agent from Scratch
headings: Write the loop before connecting a provider

concepts.title: Workflow state machine
concepts.meaning: Named states and guarded transitions constraining progress and recovery.
concepts.brief: Graph guards/checkpoints/retries; animate legal and rejected transition.
pitfalls: Retries can repeat effects without idempotency.

concepts.title: Bounded queue
concepts.meaning: Finite-capacity queue with explicit backpressure under overload.
concepts.brief: At capacity, requests wait, reject, or shed while consumers drain.
pitfalls: Bounded memory does not guarantee low latency.

concepts.title: Token bucket
concepts.meaning: Rate limiter with capped balance replenished over time and spent on admission.
concepts.brief: Bucket refills at r up to b; bursts pass until empty.
pitfalls: Average rate plus burst allowance, not fixed window.

concepts.title: Retry backoff
concepts.meaning: Retry schedule spacing transient failures with capped growth and jitter.
concepts.brief: Multiple clients recover from a 503 on spread-out jittered timelines.
pitfalls: Retry only transient, retry-safe operations.

concepts.title: Circuit breaker
concepts.meaning: Dependency guard that blocks calls after repeated failures and probes recovery.
concepts.brief: Closed/open/half-open transitions with one recovery probe.
pitfalls: Needs policy thresholds, fallback, and alerts.

concepts.title: Fallback route
concepts.meaning: Policy-controlled alternate destination used when preferred route is unavailable or ineligible.
concepts.brief: Primary/fallback lanes expose health, privacy, and cost decisions.
pitfalls: Fallback changes model, privacy, latency, and cost.

sourceRefs.title: Best AI Plans for OpenClaw in 2026
headings: Make paid fallback an explicit decision

concepts.title: Idempotency fence
concepts.meaning: Stable key or lease token preventing duplicate effects from retries or stale workers.
concepts.brief: Duplicate attempts share key; stale lease rejected at write boundary.
pitfalls: Requires atomic state and downstream deduplication.

concepts.title: Prefix trie
concepts.meaning: Tree sharing common prefixes for lookup and reuse.
concepts.brief: Token branches share cached prefix, then diverge.
pitfalls: Eviction and authorization are separate policies.

sourceRefs.title: Deep Dive - SGLang
headings: RadixAttention: prefix reuse as a tree

concepts.title: Retrieval pipeline
concepts.meaning: Stages from candidate generation through filtering, ranking, packing, and evidence use.
concepts.brief: Lexical/dense→ACL→rerank→context→citation with failure surfaces.
pitfalls: Each stage has its own denominator; evidence may be ignored.

sourceRefs.title: Context Engineering: Beyond Prompting
headings: Test whether the evidence changes the answer

concepts.title: GPU memory ledger
concepts.meaning: Accounting of weights, activations, optimizer, cache, workspaces, and reserve.
concepts.brief: Stack budget responds to batch/context/concurrency; separate training and inference.
pitfalls: Model file size is not total memory use.

sourceRefs.title: Run Gemma 4 with Ollama: Model Tags and Memory Requirements

concepts.title: Collective routing
concepts.meaning: Rank-to-rank movement satisfying distributed ownership contracts.
concepts.brief: Ranks exchange token shards to expert owners via all-to-all then return results.
pitfalls: All-to-all differs from all-gather.

sourceRefs.title: Deep Dive - NCCL
headings: Choose the operation from desired ownership

concepts.title: Kernel tiling
concepts.meaning: Processing large tensors in bounded tiles with near-compute staging and reuse.
concepts.brief: Tiles move through memory hierarchy, compute, and accumulate.
pitfalls: Tile shapes are hardware-specific; merge math must stay valid.

sourceRefs.title: Deep Dive - FlashAttention
headings: Online softmax is what makes the tiles exact

concepts.title: Latency and service metrics
concepts.meaning: Measurements separating first-token time, inter-token delay, throughput, and useful work.
concepts.brief: Timeline and fleet chart distinguish TTFT/ITL/TPOT/TPS/goodput.
pitfalls: Metrics use different denominators and windows.

headings: 11. Fleet TPS rose and users still wait. How do TTFT, ITL, TPOT, and TPS differ?
